title: Born Enslaved, He Rode 500 Miles to Prove the Army Wrong

beats.text: In June 1918, a fifty-four-year-old Army officer saddled his horse in Wilberforce, Ohio, and started riding east.

overlays.hook: He rode 497 miles to prove them wrong.

beats.text: His destination was Washington, D.C., almost five hundred miles away.
The Army had just told him he was too sick to lead men into the First World War.
He was the highest-ranking Black officer in the United States Army. And many believed the real reason he was sidelined had nothing to do with his health.
His name was Charles Young. He was born enslaved. This is his story.
Charles Young was born on March 12, 1864, in Mays Lick, Kentucky, to enslaved parents, Gabriel and Arminta Young.
The Civil War was still being fought. Within a year, his father escaped across the Ohio River.
In February 1865, Gabriel Young joined the Union Army, in the Fifth United States Colored Heavy Artillery. His service helped secure the family's freedom.

visual.caption: A call to men of color to join the Union Army, 1863

beats.text: After the war, the family settled across the river, in Ripley, Ohio.
His mother could read, and she taught him at home. He went on to study French and German, and he played the piano and the violin.
In 1881, at seventeen, he graduated with honors from Ripley's high school, the only Black student in his class.
Then he became a teacher, at the town's school for Black children.
In 1883, he sat the entrance exam for the United States Military Academy at West Point, and scored second highest.

visual.caption: Cavalry drill, U.S. Military Academy, West Point

beats.text: The next year, an Ohio congressman nominated him. In June 1884, he entered West Point.
Very few Black cadets had made it through. White cadets used what was called silencing. They would not speak to Black cadets unless they had to.
He was given a heavy load of demerits. He failed mathematics in his first year, and had to repeat it.
Near the end, he failed an engineering course. He studied all summer, took it again, and passed.
In 1889, Charles Young graduated. He was only the third Black graduate in West Point's history.

visual.sub: the third Black graduate of West Point

beats.text: The next would not come until 1936.
As a second lieutenant, he joined the Ninth Cavalry, one of the Army's Black regiments, the men known as Buffalo Soldiers.

visual.caption: A Buffalo Soldier of the Ninth Cavalry, Nebraska

beats.text: He served at Fort Robinson, Nebraska, and then at Fort Duchesne, Utah.
In 1894, he went to Wilberforce University in Ohio, a historically Black college, to teach military science.
There he became close friends with a young professor named W. E. B. Du Bois.
In 1898, during the war with Spain, he was made a major of volunteers and given command of the Ninth Ohio, a Black battalion.
The war ended before his men were sent overseas. He went back to the regular Army, and later served in the Philippines.
In the summer of 1903, Captain Young led a company of Buffalo Soldiers into the Sierra Nevada.
He was made acting superintendent of Sequoia and General Grant national parks. He was the first Black superintendent of a national park.

visual.caption: Captain Charles Young, Acting Superintendent of Sequoia National Park

beats.text: His soldiers guarded the giant trees, and built roads and trails.
By mid-August, wagons could reach the Giant Forest for the first time.
He also built a road toward Moro Rock, and urged the government to buy up private land inside the park.
In 1904, the Army sent him to Haiti, as one of its first military attaches.
For about three years, he gathered intelligence, and mapped much of Haiti and the neighboring Dominican Republic.
In 1912, he was promoted to major, the first Black man to hold that rank in the regular Army.
That year he went to Liberia, as military attache. He helped train the Liberian Frontier Force, and supervised the building of roads.
In 1916, after Pancho Villa's raid on Columbus, New Mexico, the Army sent troops into Mexico to hunt him down.
Major Young commanded a squadron of the Tenth Cavalry.
On April 1, 1916, at Agua Caliente, he led a cavalry pistol charge against Villa's forces.
They drove back about a hundred and fifty men. His squadron did not lose a single soldier.
That summer he was promoted to lieutenant colonel. The NAACP awarded him its Spingarn Medal.
In April 1917, the United States entered the First World War.
Charles Young was the highest-ranking Black officer in the Army. He was in line for promotion, and for command in France.
But some white officers said they would not take orders from a Black man.

President Woodrow Wilson heard from Southern members of Congress. He wrote to his Secretary of War, Newton Baker, about a lieutenant who found it practically impossible to serve under a colored commander.
That summer, an Army medical board examined Young. It found high blood pressure.

visual.caption: Newton D. Baker, Secretary of War

beats.text: In July 1917, he was promoted to colonel, and in the same stroke retired, as medically unfit.
He would not lead troops in the war.
So Charles Young decided to prove them wrong.

visual.caption: Colonel Charles Young's house, Wilberforce, Ohio

beats.text: On June 6, 1918, he left his home in Wilberforce on horseback.
He rode through Ohio, West Virginia, Maryland and Virginia.
On June 22, he rode into Washington. He had covered four hundred ninety-seven miles in a little over two weeks.
A Black newspaper, The Crisis, reported that he arrived in first class condition.
He met with Secretary Baker. Baker did not change the decision.
On November 6, 1918, the Army called him back to active duty, and sent him to Camp Grant, in Illinois.
Five days later, the war was over.
In 1920, he returned to Liberia as military attache.
In late 1921, on a trip to Nigeria, he fell seriously ill.
On January 8, 1922, Charles Young died at the British hospital in Lagos, of a kidney infection. He was fifty-seven.
British law required that he be buried there, for a year.
His wife and many others pressed to bring him home.
In May 1923, his body reached New York, where crowds came out to meet it.

visual.caption: A newspaper tribute to Colonel Young after his death

beats.text: On June 1, 1923, he was given a funeral in the Memorial Amphitheater at Arlington National Cemetery. He was only the fourth soldier to be honored there.

visual.caption: Funeral of Colonel Charles Young, Arlington, 1 June 1923

beats.text: He was buried at Arlington with full military honors.
W. E. B. Du Bois said the life of Charles Young was a triumph of tragedy.

visual.quote: The life of Charles Young was a triumph of tragedy.

beats.text: In 2013, his home in Wilberforce became a national monument, the Charles Young Buffalo Soldiers National Monument.

visual.caption: The Charles Young Buffalo Soldiers National Monument

beats.text: And a century after his death, the Army promoted him to brigadier general. The ceremony was held in 2022, at West Point.
He was born enslaved, and became a colonel.
He made it through West Point, guarded the giant sequoias, mapped Haiti, and led a charge in Mexico.
When the Army said he was too sick to serve, he rode nearly five hundred miles to show them otherwise.
That was Charles Young. Subscribe for more.
